utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution is continuing with examination-in-chief. Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I address the Bench on three brief matters before I continue with the examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The first is just to advise the Chamber and the registrar that sitting with the Prosecution today is another lawyer from the Prosecution's office, Mr. Jonathan Ratel, who is sitting with the Prosecution in the absence of two of the other trial members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. He's welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. The second matter is that I've spoken with the Defence counsel for Mr. Milan Simic concerning the matter of identification, and my understanding from our discussions is that Mr. Milan Simic concedes that were he to be in court, that this witness would be able to -- identify him and to that extent waives his right to be in court for court identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon. That is a correct assumption. That is what we have agreed. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You're welcome. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honour, the third matter relates to a number of documents which are the result of the proceedings against this witness in the Bijeljina court. I indicated yesterday that we were expecting the translations back. Those translations unfortunately are not back. Mr. Novak has informed me that they were submitted to the Translation Unit on the 25th of March, but due to the overwhelming tasks imposed on the translation at the moment they're not available today. They will be available by the end of the week. As a number of those documents are of interest -- well, are of interest to the Prosecution and the Defence to have the witnesses' comments on them, what we would propose is that those documents which we wish the witness to testify about would be placed on the ELMO by the witness in the B/C/S version, with a portion highlighted. That small portion could be read into the record by the witness and then commented upon with the final English version being entered into evidence when it's available at the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That's proper. It is workable that way. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I believe that's what -- okay. Then we'll proceed along that manner and hope it works. KEMAL MEHINOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mehinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: At the end of yesterday's testimony, you were speaking about one time when you were in Batkovici camp and Mr. Tadic had come to the camp and had read a list of names out of people who were to be exchanged, and your testimony was that your name was initially read out and then that you saw Mr. Sabah Seric hand to Mr. Tadic, I believe, a hundred Deutschmarks and promised him further money and that after this exchange that you witnessed had happened, that your name was no longer on the exchange list. Do you recall that testimony from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, I'd like to clarify is exactly what happened next, because you then discussed about a meeting with the warden of the camp. So could you please -- after you saw this money exchange hands, did you personally have a meeting with the camp warden and with Mr. Tadic, or did Mr. Tadic and the camp warden have meetings just among themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were together in their office because we went there for further talks. That's where approval was decided for people to go --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for a second. My earphones appear not to be working, as I'm not receiving the English translation, although my colleagues on the Bench [sic] are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So after the lists were read out, Mr. Tadic went off with the camp warden to his office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not his office; that's the camp warden's office. That's where meetings were held.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So where did Mr. Tadic and the camp warden hold this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the warden's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very sorry. I'm still getting no English translation through my earphones.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Testing, testing. Can you hear English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have a test?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three. Can you hear English now?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. I can hear it now. I apologise to the Bench. I didn't appreciate that until someone spoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, I apologise for this. It's a technical problem with my earphones. So I understand from your last answer that this meeting took place in the warden's office. Were you also in the warden's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And you said yesterday as well that he said you didn't have enough money. Who said that you had no money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both of them. Both he and the warden.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And when you say "he," who exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic told you personally that you did not have enough money to deserve to go on the exchange list; is that the essence of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. The warden had two letters of invitation sent by my family from Italy and Turkey, certifying that I have family abroad, and that was to confirm that they could expect some remuneration on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And when you protested -- or when you protested in that meeting, how did -- well, did Mr. Tadic or the camp warden react?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing. I said nothing. I was just returned to the hangar. I think it was a policeman, a local policeman, who had a nickname of "little dragon" who took me back to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you exchanged during this exchange following Mr. Tadic's visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was Sabah Seric indeed exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had left, yes. He had gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: How much longer did you stay in -- sorry. Did you see -- did you receive a visit from Mr. Tadic a second time or did you see Mr. Tadic in the camp a second time after this episode?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. If I remember correctly, it was in July 1993, when an exchange based on the all-for-all principle was to take place, on the Satorovic separation line. Out of 400 or so prisoners in the camp, only two of us from Samac remained. 180 had already been exchanged in previous exchanges over the previous several months, so that only 20 of us remained. Mr. Tadic was involved in this exchange, but he took us apart. He singled us out and left us behind in the Batkovici camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, this visit or this episode in July 1993, did Mr. Tadic himself turn up at Batkovici camp? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Had you received information prior to Mr. Tadic's arrival that an exchange would take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were so advised by the warden and the police. They said that the camp would be closed and that an all-for-all exchange would be carried out. Unfortunately, that's not what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You then said that Mr. Tadic took you apart, singled you out and left you behind. Can you describe exactly what happened on the day that you were told the exchange would occur and what exactly Mr. Tadic's actions were in singling you out and leaving you behind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the compound of the camp, within the parameter, an order was given: Muslims go to the left and Croats to the right, and people from Samac stand in the middle. I didn't know the reason, because we too were Muslims, and I don't know why we were not allowed to join the group of other Muslims, why we were singled out, but that's what happened. And when this order was given, names were read out, the names of those other people, and they boarded the buses, whereas we were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When the order was given for Muslims to go to the left, Croats to the right, and the people from Bosanski Samac to stand in the middle, where was Mr. Tadic? Was he present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was he the one who gave the instructions that people from Bosanski Samac should stand in the middle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he and the warden of the camp were standing at the gate, and the orders were announced by that policeman nicknamed "little dragon." His name was Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you ever given any explanation as to why the people from Bosanski Samac were not allowed to board the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Tadic in Batkovici camp after this episode in July 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: How much longer did you stay in Batkovici camp, Mr. Mehinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I was sent out to work to Panafleks company. Then I would be taken back to Batkovici. And immediately before my release, I was in Janja, but I was returned to Batkovici the day before my release. There were 12 of us people from Samac there. I don't know when the others had been exchanged, but there were 12 of us remaining, and we were taken to the Pale camp. It was only at 5.00 in the afternoon that we got to the Pale camp. We were supposed to be exchanged then and there, but it was late, and the ICRC took us in, talked to us and told us that we were going to be exchanged. After a while, we were put on a bus and got seated, and we were at a separation line, where Mr. Jakusi was. And during all that time that we spent at the separation line, we stayed there until 5.00 a.m., and at 5.00 a.m. we started boarding transporters headed for the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was on the 6th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So Mr. Mehinovic, is it correct that you were in detention by the Serb authorities until the 6th of October, 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And whilst you were mainly detained in Batkovici, I understand from your testimony that you've just given, that you were also taken out on forced labour duties to various other locations during the 18 months or so you spent in Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified to a day when you were brought to what appeared to be a courthouse in Bijeljina, and you were brought into a room before people who you assumed to be judges. Apart from that incident in the whole time you were detained, were you ever brought to any other judicial proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, I'd like to ask you some questions on three documents which relate to that episode in Bijeljina you told the Chamber about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And if I could ask for the usher's assistance. Your Honour, the Defence counsel have these documents and I'll now give to the usher copies to be distributed to the registry and the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe we have some technical difficulties, because we cannot see what is on the ELMO. Actually, it is a black screen here. Now it's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. The Bench has a black screen. Yes, now we are okay. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, this is a document which bears the date the 19th of January, 1993, and subject to corrections by Defence counsel, it purports to be a record of a hearing before a panel of judges by this witness that took place in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This document was given to you by the Defence or --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It was disclosed to us by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe we can have the confirmation from the Defence what this document is. Maybe it will cut down time. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these documents and several following documents that will be presented during the proceedings are actually criminal records of the court in Bijeljina in the proceedings that were conducted against this witness here. On the 26th of March I made them available to the Prosecution, and as far as I know, the Prosecution has interviewed the witness about these documents. And the only thing that is pending are translations; I'm informed they will be ready by Friday. Under the law on criminal proceedings of the SFRY, this document is a record of the questioning of the accused before the investigating judge. I believe that is written on the title -- on the cover sheet. Perhaps the Prosecution intends to elaborate on this, so I will not go into any further explanations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can I just make one correction to the record. Mr. Lukic is correct, he did disclose a number of documents to us on the 26th of March. At that time, I believe due to the clerical error, two pages of what he disclosed to us were not received. One page which I addressed the Bench on yesterday and I was allowed to approach the client, the second page which didn't come through with the documents was in fact the second page of this three-page document. And just this morning Mr. Lukic brought it to my attention that we hadn't received it because it was on the reverse side of the original documentation. So the witness will in fact, according to his evidence, never have seen one of these pages. But I'm happy to proceed just to ask him questions on it without addressing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, could I ask you to look at the document that is on the ELMO beside you. It may be easier for you to look at the actual document rather than the screen, just so you can see the whole document. Highlighted at the bottom is a signature. Does that -- do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Is it your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to turn the page over.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I just ask you to look at the signature at the bottom. Again, that page, is that also your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And finally, the third page of that document. In the middle of the page there's a third signature. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mehinovic, you've heard the Defence counsel put on the record that this purports to be a record of the hearing that took place in Bijeljina. Did you give a statement to the judge whilst you were -- when you were brought to this courthouse in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did the judge -- whilst you were in front of who you believed to be the judge, did the judge record anything and come down and make you sign -- or request you to sign a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't make any notes. I don't remember signing this, but maybe I was so afraid that I signed it without remembering.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, could I ask you to look now at the second page of the document, and there will be a portion at the bottom which is highlighted. Could I ask you to read out very slowly on to the record, as best as you can read the document, what it says in that highlighted paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The accused is informed that he has been assigned defence counsel ex officio Ziko Krunic, attorney from Bijeljina. The request for the conducting of an investigation by the military prosecutor's office of Bijeljina."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The numbers are unclear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Number 22/52, dated 4th of January, 1993, is read out.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. What you've just read out says that you have been assigned an attorney from Bijeljina by the name of Ziko Krunic. Have you ever heard the name Ziko Krunic before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Have you ever met any person called Ziko Krunic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you at any time told that you had a lawyer assigned to you by the name of Ziko Krunic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Before being in this courtroom today, have you ever read that paragraph in this document which you just read out to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer to that question? I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't had it so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, could I ask you now to look at the third page of that document, and again at the bottom there is a paragraph which is highlighted, and I'd be grateful if you could read out slowly, for the benefit of the interpreters, so that the Chamber knows what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "An investigation will be conducted against the accused Kemal Mehinovic, son of Muradif, from Bosanski Samac, on well-grounded suspicion that he has committed the crime, suspicion that he committed a crime from Article 124, paragraph 1, and related to Article 139, paragraph 3, taken over from the Penal Code of the SFRY in the manner indicated in the request for investigation. The present decision has been notified to the accused, who states that he waives his right to appeal. The decision is notified to the accused, who states that he waives his right to appeal and does not require the decision to be overturned." I do not wish to read the minutes. My statement has been recorded truthfully, or faithfully, which I confirm with my signature."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I might be -- Your Honours, I might be wrong, but my English is not my native language. But I believe that the last -- it's 13 -- page 13, row 3. "Require the decision to be overturned." Actually, what it says is that the person does not wish that the written copy is handed to him, so he waives the right -- because he's waiving the right to appeal. He is also waiving the right to receive a written copy to be handed over to him. I don't know whether the "overturned" is exactly what it does say in the original. If the translators can - I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters apologise. This word was really unclear to us and the "overturning" was a guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So what, according to the interpreters, what is the correct version, then?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters simply don't know. I'm sorry. What counsel is saying may be completely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. We'll proceed, because we are going to have the English translation anyway, so we'll deal with it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, did you waive your right to appeal -- were you advised of any decision that had been taken against you whilst you were in any of the rooms in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally am sure that I did not waive my right to appeal, because based on all these things, from what I know, it is death penalty that is the penalty for this, and I don't believe there is any such person that would sign their own death penalty.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you ever asked -- were you ever advised that you had a right to appeal any decision taken by that panel you appeared in front of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, the first part of your question at line 25: "Were you advised of any decision that had been taken against you?" hasn't been answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, could I ask you to address that same question again? Did anyone ever advise you that a decision -- that there was a well-grounded suspicion that you had committed a crime against Article 124 and related to Article 139 had been made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And I understand from your last answer that you were never advised that you had any right to appeal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And did you at any stage, then, waive -- yourself decide that you would waive a right to appeal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you ever advised that you had a right to have a copy of any decision that was reached against you, given a copy of that decision handed over to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you ever indicate to anybody in the courtroom that you waived any right to have any copies of decisions given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you ever state to anyone in the room of which you were -- which you were called into that you had no desire or you did not wish to read any minutes that were taken of the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you ever asked by anyone in the room whether or not you wanted to review minutes of proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was your statement recorded whilst you were in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not while I was there. This name, first and last name of the person who was taking the notes, I see for the first time, and on the right-hand side, from the decision, there is no signature of the investigative judge. Therefore, I do not consider this decision to be legally binding.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mehinovic. If you can just answer my questions on the document, and we'll leave the other conclusions to be drawn. Did you ever state that your statement had been recorded truthfully or faithfully or did you ever see -- were you ever presented with a copy of your statement which you acknowledged to be a truthful and faithful recording?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, when was the first time that you saw this document which -- from which you've just read --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here at The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: At no stage during your period of detention did you ever read any part of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation as to how your signature came to be upon it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said before, when I was at the so-called court, there were only two or three words that were exchanged, and I don't quite remember whether it was that I signed this here or in the hall, when the police officer was supposed to take me to the correctional centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, is your testimony that you don't remember signing anything at all or that you remember signing something but you're not sure whether it was in the hall or where you might have signed something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So you cannot recall whether or not you signed something at all; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I have a second document which I'd like to be shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have it numbered first for identification purposes only.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It will be document P55 ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: For identification only, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Your Honours. It's P55 ID ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is another document which we received from Defence counsel for Mr. Tadic, and for the record, it purports to be a receipt for the handover of certain documents to Mr. -- to a Mr. Kemal Mehinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, if you see that document on the ELMO, in the centre of the page there is a word in Cyrillic highlighted. Could you just read that out into the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Receipt."

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: On the right-hand corner of that document, there is a place for a signature and there's a faint name. Can you read out, to the best of your ability, what appears on the right-hand corner of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first line, I can read a signature, Mehinovic, and the second part, however, is very blurry. I don't think this is the original of the signature. I didn't -- I mean, I disagree with the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether it's my signature or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You're saying -- so the name on the right-hand corner, you do not positively recognise as your signature; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, up in the left-hand corner there's also a highlighted line. Could you read out what is highlighted there on the top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, it says "March 27th."

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you recall whether sometime in March you were ever handed any sort of documents relating to trial proceedings in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did anyone ever give you any documents relating to decisions taken against you in Bijeljina or to the assignment of counsel to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you ever remember signing any receipt acknowledging acceptance of delivery of documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: At any time on the 27th of March 1993, or at any time in 1993 and 1994, did someone come to you in Batkovici and give you documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not receive any. It might the case that I was working at the time, but I didn't receive any documents, nor do I know that anybody came to give me documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honours, again could I ask that this be given an identification number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have a number for identification only, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is P56 ter ID, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the third and final document of this nature I'd like to put to the witness. I'm afraid the copy itself is quite faint, and I'm hoping that we will be able to read out just the important parts to advise the Chamber what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The copy which is given to the witness is as bad as these copies?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: If Your Honours are able to see the ELMO, you will see that when portions which I'd ask the witness to read out are highlighted, it does make the writing that little bit more visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. You can proceed. Yes, you can proceed, if the witness will be able to read. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, again you'll see a document on the ELMO, and there will be a portion in it which is highlighted. Could I ask you again to read out, as best as you're able to - and please read it slowly so that the interpreters can catch the interpretation - what that highlighted portion of this document says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Decision terminating the criminal proceedings against the accused Mehinovic Kemal, son of Muradif, born on the 6th of May, 1956, in Bosanski Samac, residing in Vuk Karadzic Street number 64. For the crime of armed insurgency based on Article 124, paragraph 1 relating to the Article 135, act 3..." These two things I cannot discern. "Because the law amending the law on amnesty, public gazette of Republika Srpska number 17 through 39 -- through 99 was relieved of prosecution."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can confirm that the witness read the text; however, the first two words that the witness read, therefore -- I have a much better copy. Therefore, I would like to read the first two words again. I would like to suggest that the witness do it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The criminal proceedings against the accused Kemal Mehinovic is being terminated. He's the son of Muradif, born on May 6th, 1956 in Bosanski Samac and resides in Vuk Karadzic Street number 64. For the crime of armed insurgence see based on Article 124, paragraph 1, relating to the Article 135, Act 3, KZRS because the law amending the law on amnesty S1 gazette of RS number 17 through 99 of July 15th, 1999 was relieve of prosecution."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the purposes of accuracy, it's the Article 139 and not 135. It says armed insurgency according to Article 134 paragraph 1 in connection to Article 139, paragraph 2 or 3. I don't know. I don't see it. And the transcript it's 135. So if the witness can read again, because he has a much better copy than I have on the ELMO. But I know it's 139.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to save the witness reading it, we're willing to concede it's 139.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, could I ask you to turn again to the document on the ELMO that you've just been reading from, or maybe indeed you could keep your eye on the better copy that the Defence provided you with. Can you see a date on this document in the top left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The date is March 22nd, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, were you advised that criminal proceedings had been terminated against you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When was the first time that you learnt of this decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And again, I'd just ask that that be given a number for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have a number for identification purposes only.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I apologise, Your Honours. It seems that we've been having a problem with the electric microphone. We have the technicians on it right now. It will be document P57 ter ID.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, you have told the Chamber that you were finally released in October 1994. In which place in Bosnia were you actually released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Sarajevo. I had an exchange in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And ultimately, Mr. Mehinovic, where did you end up living, or where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I live in the United States now, in Salt Lake City, in Utah.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: After you were detained in Bosanski Samac, what happened to your wife and your son and your daughter? Did they remain in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were exchanged, I think in July of 1993. The location of the exchange was Dragalicevo, on the Croatian side. Orasje, that belonged to Croatia, to the HVO. They took in my family until I arrived from the exchange in 1994. Towards the end of 1994/early 1995, I asked for help in Osijek from UNHCR. There I was informed that I can leave Croatia and ask to be resettled into another country. From them I received all the possible documentation, also paid transportation to the United States.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, did you ever discuss with your wife her exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I wasn't able to, nor did I have the opportunity. When I met up with my wife, she told me that she had not wanted to be exchanged because I was still in a camp at the time, and she thought it would have been better for her to stay in Samac in expectation of my release.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. So can I just clarify something, Mr. Mehinovic. At the time I understand you did not have the opportunity to discuss your wife's exchange, but after she was exchanged and after you were reunited with your family, did you have an opportunity to discuss with her her exchange and what had happened to her after you had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And if she told you that she didn't want to be exchanged because she didn't know what your fate was, why was it that she was exchanged in Dragalic in 1993. Did she explain to you how that came about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The explanation is simple: They were not able to stay there because a large group of people from Bosanski Samac was taken for an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I ask that the witness be shown a document? This is a list of persons to be exchanged in Dragalic. I believe it contains the name of this witness's wife and his children and other persons, and we have an English translation of it. So perhaps the B/C/S could be put on the ELMO beside the witness and the English translations distributed to the Bench --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: -- and the legal officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, can you see to your right there a document which purports to be a list of persons to cross into Croatia for an exchange planned on the 15th of June, 1993, in Dragalic? Do you see that document beside you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I ask you to turn to the second page of that document, second page in the B/C/S version, and to look down the left-hand column, and you'll see names beside the number 46, a name Fazila Mehinovic. Do you know Fazila Mehinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's my wife.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you advise the Chamber who the next five persons under the name of your wife are, the next five persons, down to the number 52?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my wife's sister and her children. My children are under numbers 51 and 52. Damir and Elvira Mehinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us how old your children were at the time of this exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My son was about 15 and my daughter 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I think those were the only questions I have to ask the witness. He won't be familiar with the list otherwise. Could I ask that it be entered into evidence and be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think there's no objection from the Defence. Can we have the document as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It will be P58 for the English translation and P58 ter for the B/C/S version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one final document to show the witness. It's a document that we have an English translation of, but I think it would serve the Bench better when they have the document in front of them that I explain what it is. Your Honours, this is a list of persons of Muslim and Croat nationality left in Bosanski Samac. As you see, we've provided a translation of it, and because the document, which is four pages, is in essence a list of names, going from numbers 1 through to 277, what the Translation Unit have done is just to pick out those names on the list where there appear something more than just the name of the person. So, for example, at number 22, the name Sehapovic Ahmet, it says "and child." So is the Bench clear on how the Translation Unit have approached this translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, except -- yes. These names on the -- what are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. called the English list is an extract from the Serbo-Croat list, and it just shows some extra information about certain names. What I want to know is: The list says of Muslims and Croats in Bosanski Samac. Is it -- at what stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is indeed a problem. The document was given to us by both sources, people who had worked from the Serbian commission of exchanges and also those on the Croatian side who had received persons who formerly lived in Bosanski Samac. The document came to us in this format, and unfortunately it doesn't have a date on it, which does mean that it's not clear when this was. Now, this witness's name appears on this list, the wife -- the names of his wife and children and that don't. So I'm afraid that the Prosecution had simply stated that -- this was at some stage after July 1993, and we're in a position we can say -- we don't know exactly when -- what date this list was drawn up and except that it was -- it appears to be after July -- after June 1993, and certainly prior to this witness being released from custody or being transferred to Batkovici. But I'm afraid both copies were given to the Prosecution without a date indicated, and we realise that that has an impact on the weight which the Bench can attach to it, but we would like to have it in evidence nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What's the purpose of having it in evidence? What is it supposed to show?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, you'll know that the Prosecution case is that from 17.000 or more Bosnians and Muslims who used to live in Bosanski Samac, that by this process of what we've termed so-called exchanges and other means, that the Bosnian and -- that the Muslim and Croat population in Bosanski Samac, at the end of this process, had dwindled to just under 300, and that is a figure that we came up with from the evidence available to the Prosecution. This is one of those pieces -- this was a document where it is purported they have listed the remaining Bosnian -- and the commissions drew up a list of the remaining persons [Realtime transcript read in error "Americans"] in Bosanski Samac who had Muslim or Croat ethnicity. As I said, I know that as a document it has its flaws, and therefore the weight to be given to it must be carefully considered by the Bench, but we would like to have it in evidence for what it's worth as it is part of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, the problem is it has no date, and from your explanation, why don't you call the sources of the document to give evidence on it? Because this witness can't explain anything about this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but the witness can identify that his name appears on the list. He does also have information as to other persons from this list who are of -- supposedly of Croat and Muslim origin and who this list purports -- are still remaining in Bosanski Samac. This list has been disclosed to all Defence counsel for a couple of years now, and we've never had any challenge to it as it being in any way less than authentic. And I said the sources were both -- we got this document from both a Serb source and a Croat source. These were exchanges going on about persons living in the area and presumably involved in the whole process of swapping population figures and names in exchanges. So as I said, Your Honour, we know it is a flawed document, but we do consider that we would like to see it in evidence and the appropriate weight to be attributed to it in the final overall evaluation when the Prosecution case rests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First of all, -- sorry. Yes. Thank you. Your Honours, in fact, I would like to intervene. It's page 26, line 5. It's something a little bit unlogic, unclear. "A list of remaining Americans in Bosanski Samac who had Muslim or Croat ethnicity." Maybe it's not the case. So it's just intervention in order to clear up the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: To correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But about the submission of our learned friends from the Prosecution, maybe we could add something later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, what's the correct -- what is it supposed to be? How should it read correctly?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Well, it certainly shouldn't read "Americans," so I'm happy to go with persons of -- I think persons of Muslim and Croat ethnicity is probably the appropriate term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought I saw some other counsel. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I suggest that for now we give this document only a number for identification. First of all, I believe that this document was only partially delivered to the Prosecution -- in fact, sorry, it was made available to the Prosecution by only one side, the Serbian side, not the Croatian side, and that also bears on the weight to be attached to this evidence. And some of the facts stated by my colleague from the Prosecution, such as that there were only 17.000 Croats and Muslims in Samac are not quite true. There were in total 5.000 citizens of all nationalities in Samac. This list purports to be a list of people located in Bosanski Samac. That's why I believe that it would be worthwhile to call the person who made this list available to the Prosecution, and I believe it was only one side, not both sides, that presented the list. But that is something that I can confirm only after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to have it marked for identification purposes now -- I'm sorry. Your Honour, I'm happy to have it marked for identification purposes now, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You'll deal with matters that have been raised later.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Exactly. And further witnesses may be able to comment and throw light on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Essentially -- okay. I think we'll have the one in Serbo-Croat marked as usual and the one in English will have its own number, for both identification purposes only.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the B/C/S version will be P59 ter ID and the English version P59 ID. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Reidy. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, can I ask you to look at the document on the ELMO, and perhaps you could turn to the third page of the document. Mr. Mehinovic, at number 171, does your name appear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was there any other Kemal Mehinovic living in Bosanski Samac at the time, that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. I'm the only Kemal Mehinovic in Bosanski Samac. Apart from my family, that is, the family of my father, there is -- there are no other Mehinovics in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you know anyone by the name of Hasan Mehinovic, the name that appears below yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no such name in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, did I ask you to have a look through this list at the weekend when you arrived in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you recognise a lot of the names that appear on this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And of those you were able to recognise, did most of them come from Bosanski Samac, or did all of them come from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them -- all of these people are from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Out of the names listed, did you recognise a lot of those names as persons that you knew to be members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: On the page on which your name appears, could you perhaps just indicate by reference to the numbers any of those people who you said were with the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Mehinovic, I'll ask you to stop there. I think you've given us some indication of the number. Before you came to The Hague, had you ever been shown this list before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to ascertain from the witness from that list for the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, so that you were finally able to move to the United States, is it the case that since you've been in the United States, that you initiated a lawsuit based on some of the things that happened to you in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was that a criminal case or a civil case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A civil case.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And who was the civil case against?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Against Nikola Vukovic, also known as Batan.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was Nikola Vukovic also in America at the time that you instigated this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: How did you know that he was in America at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in keeping with the ruling of the Trial Chamber made last week, we are talking here about the period of time which goes far beyond the indictment. I mean, the questions that are being asked by the Prosecution now, and I believe also the questions are being asked about persons who are irrelevant for our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only reason I go down this route is because this is a case which Defence counsel have frequently brought into issue here. They have -- particularly Defence counsel for Mr. Milan Simic raised it and in fact asked this Bench to take judicial notice of the initial filing by lawyers of this civil case. We now have before us the primary witness who initiated that suit. I only intend to ask a few questions. I don't need to, if the Chamber considers this wholly irrelevant, I'm happy to stop. That is the only reason I led evidence on this at all, because of what has already arisen in this case, initiated by Defence counsel. So if they're not going to raise the case with this or any other witness, then of course I will not lead on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can go ahead, for whatever it's worth.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, the question I asked you was just: How did you know that Mr. Vukovic was in America at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through a friend who lives in the same city and works for the same company. He called me and said, "Your friend Batan is in Atlanta."

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: During those proceedings that you started, how many times did you ever make a statement to the court about your -- what happened to you in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One day when both of us -- both he and I were summoned, together with many witnesses, we appeared before the court, and that's when our case was discussed. But there was a period before that during which my lawyers were engaged on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: This one day, when was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was in the year 2001, towards the end of the year. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Vukovic actually in the courtroom --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Vukovic actually in the courtroom when your case was discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He didn't show up, nor were his counsel there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you successful in the case against Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Vukovic the only defendant in the case in the United States?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mehinovic, just to finish your examination, I'd like to ask you some questions pertaining to any long-term injuries or medical complications you may have sustained as a result of what you experienced during detention in Bosanski Samac. Could you advise the Chamber whether or not you -- or after you had been released, whether you required any form of medical intervention or medical treatment as a result of injuries or complications you sustained following from your detention in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I was exchanged in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I had no occasion to see a doctor. There were not enough doctors. And moreover, I didn't have enough money. However, when I arrived in the States, via Croatia, I was entitled to medical assistance and I went through first check-ups, and they confirmed my original suspicions about some dark areas in my abdomen and elsewhere in my body. Until 1999, I continued working; however, one morning I was unable to get up, and paramedics arrived, together with my doctor, who said, "You'll have to see me one of these days and we'll have to do something urgently." On the 11th of January 2000, I underwent four surgeries in six days. Half of my stomach was extracted, and eight centimetres in one section of my intestines and eight centimetres of another intestine and half of a kidney. I have proof, and my doctors can confirm, that these injuries were due to blows and that I had in those areas dark stains which could be seen on x-rays and scans. These parts of organs had to be taken out. I have to this day problems with my ribs and my head. On the back of my head, there is a fissure, five centimetres long and two centimetres deep. To this day I have frequent pains, for which I take painkillers. Thank you very much. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll have a break and continue our proceedings at 1615 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just be a few minutes more, Your Honours, and then I intend to close the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, before the break you told the Chamber of various medical treatments you've undergone. Are you required now to constantly take medication for your ailments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Have your doctors indicated to you that that medication -- you'll have to take that medication for the foreseeable future?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, I now want to finally ask you about what happened to the flats and the two restaurants that you and your brother owned, which we saw in the photograph entered into evidence as Prosecution Exhibit P53. When your wife and your children were forced to partake in the exchange in June 1993, were they told what was going to happen -- or were they allowed to take with them all the possessions that were in your flat in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not allowed to take anything. There was a military policeman called Naser Sejdic, and there was another colleague of his who made a record and a list of the property, of my entire property. They were only allowed to take one bag. My wife was allowed to take this one bag to have a change of clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was your wife given a copy of this record or list of property which was made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was your wife told what would happen to the property which was recorded on this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Have you ever since then received back or received any information about what happened to the property that was put onto that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found out that the majority of my property was thrown out or dispersed, and later, first there was a police command in my apartment, and also -- on my side and on my brother's side, and after that they moved out, and then they allowed other persons to move in who were families of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: From whom did you find out that your property had been thrown out or dispersed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my friends who came to the States and who were longer in Bosanski Samac than I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Have you made any attempt to reclaim or get compensation for your property or your businesses and flats which you had to give up in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Last year my brother went to Bosanski Samac. I gave him a power of attorney for my property, so that he could start proceedings to have my property returned. In the meantime, he got his part of the house, but he did not get my part of the house because he said that the power of attorney was no longer valid and that I had to go there by myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did your brother get any of his possessions back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My brother got his part of the house back and also his establishment. In the part where my establishment used to be, my friend, Uros Cane was located. In the meantime, he closed the establishment. He won't give the key to anyone. The establishment no longer operates. And a woman with her child is living in my apartment currently.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did your brother get any of his movable possessions back in addition to the physical house and the establishment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was none left.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And did your brother ever receive any compensation for any things that he had lost or that had been destroyed or that had been taken away from his properties in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Mehinovic, would you yourself ultimately like to go back to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you say that you exercised your free choice to leave Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you want to leave Bosanski Samac in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did your wife or your children want to leave Bosanski Samac in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, calls for speculation. How can he know when he was in prison what was the idea of his wife and his children?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps wife and husband are one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps wife and husband are one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You don't understand what I'm saying. Perhaps husband and wife are one so he --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Probably, but she should somehow rephrase the question whether he was told by his wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: By his wife, yes. Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've already covered this in my examination. I've asked the witness whether or not since he was reunited with his family did he discuss her exchange and that, and I didn't ask, I think, you know specifically this, but I think the fact that they talked about it and some of the circumstances are already on the record. So I think the ground is already laid as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: -- context or how he could answer that question. Indeed, Your Honour, that is my final question in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Cross-examination. Who is going to start. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Mehinovic. I am going to ask you a number of questions in the cross-examination section. Before I begin this cross-examination, I would like to ask you, and I'm also going to make sure that my questions are formulated in such a way, I would like you to answer me as short as possible so that we can finish this section as soon as we can. I would like your answers to be "yes," "no," or "I don't know" if you do not know anything about the circumstances in question. I would also like to remind you, and I'd also like to remind myself, that the two of us here are speaking and understanding the same language, but it is necessary for the interpreters to interpret both my questions and your answers to other participants, and therefore I would like to ask you to make a short pause before you start responding so that the interpreters can catch up; otherwise there will be an overlap. I would like to ask you a number of questions about the conditions in Bosanski Samac before you were confined, while you were still under the labour obligation and you were moving around the town. You answered the Prosecution's questions once by saying that the water supply system was broken. Could you please tell me when that water supply system was broken and how long there was no water.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date when the water supply system was broken, and I also don't know when it was restarted, because I was taken to Batkovici. While I was there, there was no water.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the entire -- your stay until you were taken to Batkovici, there was no water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me the situation regarding water -- electricity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Same. There was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask counsel to be more clear, to ascertain more clarity as to this water supply system. Because the witness testified to the fact that there was no water whilst he was already in detention, while he was in the SUP building and that building had no water in the toilet. And if Mr. Novak is talking about general conditions, then I think it's important to clarify that this information about the water was -- the witness has testified only about when he was in detention, and I think what's on the record now is not clear that it relates to that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Mr. Lukic can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the remark of the Prosecutor. My first question was: Before he was incarcerated, in the period before he was incarcerated in Bosanski Samac, while he was still under the work obligation, was there no water then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was no water. We were bringing water from the artesian well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did any citizens of Samac have water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what the situation was with electricity? Were there any cuts of electricity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first day, there was electricity. I don't remember the time or the date, but later there was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately whether this was after a month that there was no more electricity, ten days, fifteen days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think it was maybe three to four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, several days after April 17th, there was no more electricity in Samac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume that there was also no electricity for all the citizens of Samac equally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there any shelling of Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were those shellings frequent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first days, yes, they were. That also happened maybe four or five days, there was shellings then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume there was a lot of damaged buildings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the area of the embankment, Vjenac JNA, from what I know, yes. I could only see that because that's where I was working. I don't know anything about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us more about this area of embankment? From what area were these shellings coming from? Could you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But opposite from this embankment there was this territory was under the situation -- under the rule of the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to use the numbers from the unofficial transcript, because we haven't received the official transcript yet. On page 12, during your statements yesterday, while you were describing your movements in the morning of April 17th of 1992, you said that you saw your fellow citizens, Ibela Bicic and some other civilians, and you went into the streets with them, went towards the department store, and then joined them in their movement towards the school.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These people that you saw, how many were there, approximately? Can you make an assumption?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I already said this once. I think there were about 20 people. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they have automatic rifles? Or let me ask you in a more simple way. Did they have both rifles and automatic rifles? Did you see that somebody had that type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw rifles, the so-called PAPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You already stated several times yesterday that at that moment you did not have any weapons with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you went into the streets, you described that your brother warned you not to leave the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that he came to my establishment, to my bakery, and told me, "What? Are you crazy? Where are you going? Can't you see it's war?" And then I returned home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you feel any fear when your brother told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you still did not stay in the bakery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, of course not. I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also stated that you heard Mr. Ibela Salkic saying that there was a massacre of citizens in Donja Mahala and that they were going there to defend them, and that's why you went with them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After April 17th, did you hear anything about that massacre, what kind of a massacre it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that that day or on a later day there was any massacre at all in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that somebody was murdered on April 17th of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, I didn't hear anything, but I did hear something about that on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many people were killed on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, in Donja Mahala, one person was killed. This was a person of Croatian ethnicity. He was called Ropo Dzebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This was the only death, forced death, so to speak, in the period of 17th, 18th, in Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In responding to the Prosecutor, you didn't say this, but I'm asking you now: Why did you go with these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I was curious, and also because of my security, because I wanted to know where to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were told to go back home, you weren't curious any more to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This whole event and your movements on April 17th was described in the same way to Milos Savic and here in front of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I compared it, and these are really identical facts, except that you are claiming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can I have the statement directly from the record? This is the counsel now putting his comments on the record. I've compared these are identical. He's making assertions. If he wants to ask the witness some question, he can, but that phrase is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Lukic. The objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have read the statement in front of the Chamber before you testified that was also found at -- by -- with Milos Savic. Are there any differences in what you said there and what you said here, except for the part where you claim that you weren't carrying arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there is no difference except that I was not carrying any arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's how I understood you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also when you were describing the work obligation, you said that you were digging trenches, as far as I understand, in Pisari. Were you digging trenches anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the embankment in Bosanski Samac. I showed you on the map. That was digging trenches and also building bunkers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you were also digging trenches in Pisari. That you said at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was the separation line with the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did this separation line also reach the village of Zaselica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, because I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you gave the statement to inspector Savic in July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 67 of yesterday's transcript, you also said that you saw Tadic at one occasion while you were incarcerated at the TO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When there was an exchange planned, and the Prosecutor asked you what the people that were detained there looked like, and then you described two people that you know were injured while you were there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you also said you are not personally familiar with the issue whether prisoners were exchanging clothes or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But then on page 62, you said that, when the Prosecutor asked you whether the family could through guards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may be a problem with the transcript, but the question of counsel that "you are not personally familiar with the issue whether prisoners were exchanging clothes or not" appears to my reading that could be the prisoners were exchanging clothes amongst themselves or something. I think what the witness testified to was that he did not know after prisoners were taken away whether or not they were given some sort of clean clothes. They just left in the same clothes they came in with. After that, during the exchange he couldn't know whether they were given clean clothes. I would just like it to be clarified, because for me that question whether the prisoners were exchanging clothes or not could refer to a completely different action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's a bit misleading, Mr. Lukic. Can you rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read to the witness what he said on the page 69, because the translation is also unclear to me, and through that, through his statement, we could clear this up what he said. When asked, on page 69, line 8, when asked by the Prosecutor whether Mr. Tadic could see whether the prisoners had clean clothes, he said, and I will read this in English. [In English] "I personally don't know if they received or changed clothes, but from the TO, they left. They went out wearing the same clothes that they had when they first arrived." [Interpretation] That's what the transcript says, and therefore I would like to ask you to clarify. Relevant to the prisoners that were imprisoned at the TO building, did they go through the exchange dressed the same way as you saw them when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were taken from my room wearing the same clothes that they had on. They were taken to the buses. The bus was in front of the doors of the TO building. And what happened later, I have no idea. Whether they were changing clothes later or not, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you, on page 62, whether the families could bring food and clothes through the guards. You said yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After June or July, that was being allowed a little bit, because we all said to our guards that we had lice and that we had yellow jaundice.
